Empirical Research Plan: “Health, Longevity, and Aggregate Economic Activity, 1900–2000”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen strategy: Shift–share instrumental-variables difference-in-differences (SS-IV-DID) implemented in a two-way fixed–effects panel.

Why this strategy is appropriate  
a) The epidemiological transition was a world-wide “event” that began sharply around 1940, but the size of the shock differed systematically with countries’ pre-1940 disease profiles.  
b) A shift–share (a.k.a. Bartik) instrument exploits that heterogeneity: countries that had high 1930 mortality from diseases for which global mortality fell most after 1940 should experience the largest exogenous life-expectancy gains.  
c) The DID component (country and decade fixed effects) nets out all time-invariant country traits and all global decade shocks.  
d) Remaining variation is plausibly exogenous, satisfies the exclusion restriction (disease-specific global mortality declines have no direct effect on aggregate output except through domestic health), and is highly relevant.

Formally  

First-stage:  
ΔLE_ct = π · PredictedΔLE_ct  + λ_c + δ_t + ε_ct

Second-stage (main outcome Y):  
Y_ct = β · ĤΔLE_ct  + λ_c + δ_t + X′_ct γ + u_ct     (λ_c = country FE, δ_t = decade FE)

where PredictedΔLE_ct is the shift–share instrument described below and ĤΔLE_ct is the fitted value from the first stage.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definition
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
ΔLE_ct = change in life expectancy at birth for country c between decades t–1 and t (or level LE_ct, depending on spec).

Instrument (PredictedΔLE_ct)  
PredictedΔLE_ct = Σ_d (Mortality_c,d,1938 / Pop_c,1938) × (ΔLogGlobalMortality_d,t)  
• d indexes the 15 infectious diseases.  
• The “share” is each country’s 1938 age-adjusted death rate from disease d.  
• The “shift” is the decade-t world log mortality change for disease d (constructed from WHO & League of Nations tables, common to all countries).

Control group / counterfactual  
Countries with low pre-1940 infectious-disease mortality receive little predicted shock, functioning as controls within the panel. The identifying variation is thus within-decade, across-country differences in predicted improvements.

Treatment timing  
Global mortality declines start in the 1940–49 decade. To maximize power while preserving a clean pre-period we stack balanced 10-year panels 1900–39 (pre) and 1940–2000 (post).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance: Countries with higher baseline disease burden experienced larger subsequent gains in life expectancy (first-stage F ≫ 10). Plausible given the massive disease-specific breakthroughs.

A2. Exclusion: Conditional on country and decade FE, baseline mortality interacted with global disease trends affects economic outcomes only through domestic life expectancy, not via other channels (e.g., malaria eradication raises GDP only because it raises health). Plausible because disease-specific global trends are not driven by contemporaneous country policies, but we will test.

A3. Parallel trends / common shocks: In the absence of the epidemiological transition, high- and low-burden countries would have followed parallel paths in GDP and population. We can partially test by estimating pre-1940 event-study coefficients; visually, they should be flat.

A4. Stable composition / no migration spillovers: Population movements between countries do not invalidate inference. Plausible at the country level; we will show robustness excluding large migration episodes.

A5. No anticipation: Countries could not foresee disease-specific global mortality collapses in the 1930s and change economic policy in advance. Reasonable given the suddenness of antibiotics/DDT discoveries.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Baseline disease burden correlated with other growth determinants (e.g., colonial status, institutions).  
Mitigation:  
• Country FE soak up time-invariant confounders.  
• Control vector X_ct (schooling, investment rate, war dummies).  
• Show robustness to dropping former colonies, OECD members, etc.

Threat 2: Post-1940 country-specific shocks (WWII destruction, oil discoveries) correlated with predicted health gains.  
Mitigation:  
• Decade FE remove global shocks; add region-decade FE.  
• Exclude countries with direct WWII battle damage or oil shocks and re-estimate.

Threat 3: Violation of exclusion due to disease-specific programs influencing productivity directly (e.g., DDT spraying may raise agricultural yields).  
Mitigation:  
• Drop malaria from the instrument and re-run.  
• Use alternative instrument constructed only from bacterial diseases (penicillin/streptomycin) where no plausible productivity channel exists.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)     # fast two-way FE
library(ivreg)      # IV estimation
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# 1. Load and merge data ---------------------------------------------------
pan <- fread("country_decade_panel.csv")         # main macro variables
dis <- fread("disease_mortality_1938.csv")       # 1938 mortality by disease
glob <- fread("global_mortality_by_disease.csv") # decade global shifts

# 2. Construct shift–share instrument -------------------------------------
# Merge 1938 country shares with global shifts, multiply and sum
setkey(dis, iso3); setkey(glob, disease, decade)
ss <- dis[ , .(iso3, disease, share = mort_1938)]  # mortality share

# expand to decades
decades <- unique(glob$decade)
ss <- ss[CJ(iso3 = iso3, disease = disease, decade = decades, unique = TRUE), on = .(iso3, disease)]
ss <- ss[glob, on = .(disease, decade)][ , pred_component := share * shift]
Z <- ss[ , .(Predicted_dLE = sum(pred_component, na.rm = TRUE)), by = .(iso3, decade)]

# 3. Merge instrument into panel ------------------------------------------
pan <- merge(pan, Z, by = c("iso3", "decade"))
pan <- pan[order(iso3, decade)]
pan[ , dLE := LE - shift(LE), by = iso3]           # life-expectancy change

# 4. Main IV regression ----------------------------------------------------
iv_main <- feols(gdp_pc ~ 1 | iso3 + decade | dLE ~ Predicted_dLE, data = pan,
                 cluster = ~iso3)

summary(iv_main, se = "cluster")

# 5. Robustness: drop malaria from instrument ------------------------------
malaria_free <- ss[disease != "Malaria"][ , 
       .(Pred_dLE_noMal = sum(pred_component, na.rm = TRUE)), by = .(iso3, decade)]
pan <- merge(pan, malaria_free, by = c("iso3", "decade"))
iv_nomal <- feols(gdp_pc ~ 1 | iso3 + decade | dLE ~ Pred_dLE_noMal, data = pan,
                  cluster = ~iso3)
etable(iv_main, iv_nomal)

# 6. Event-study pre-trend check (re-scaling decades around 1940) ----------
pan[ , rel_time := decade - 1940]
es <- feols(gdp_pc ~ i(rel_time, Treated, ref = -1) | iso3 + decade, data = pan,
            cluster = ~iso3)
iplot(es)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory offers two competing channels:  
• Larger, healthier labour force → higher total GDP (positive).  
• Malthusian or capital-dilution effects → ambiguous or negative effect on GDP per capita, especially in medium-run.

Prior:  
β_population > 0 and sizable (elasticity ≈ 0.8).  
β_GDP_total > 0 (elasticity ≈ 1).  
β_GDP_per_capita ≈ 0 or slightly negative (–0.3 to 0.1) within first three decades; may turn positive only after 1970s.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV context)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1  Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10):                         1  
C2  Exclusion restriction plausibility:                         0.5  
C3  No differential pre-trends (event-study flat pre-1940):     0.8  
C4  Stable unit treatment value (no cross-country spillovers):  0.7  
C5  Robustness to alternative instruments / samples:            0.8  

Overall (average) validity score ≈ 0.76 — credible but not bullet-proof.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
End of plan
